extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy (ethics); scholars studying Aristotle
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic exposition (Book I of the Nicomachean Ethics) defining the Chief Good (Happiness) and listing the necessary attributes/conditions that make a life happy, with discussion of related goods, methods of inquiry, and requirements for virtue and external goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as the Chief Good / final end
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is the end of all things which are and may be done; it is chosen always for its own sake and never with a view to anything further.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle insists the Chief Good must be 'absolutely final' — an object of choice always in itself and never as a means. Examples (wealth, pleasure, honour) are shown not to be final because they are chosen for other ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolutely final (finality) criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: That which is an object of choice always in itself, and never with a view to any other, is 'absolutely final.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text distinguishes final ends from instrumental ends and uses this as a test for the Chief Good: if something is chosen for the sake of something else, it is not absolutely final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The final good should be self-sufficient: 'which taken alone makes life choice-worthy, and to be in want of nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Self-sufficiency is not solitary existence but includes those necessary relations (parents, children, friends, countrymen). Limits must be fixed to avoid endless expansion of what counts as self-sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Activity of the soul in accordance with reason/virtue (function argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work of man is a working of the soul in accordance with reason; the Good of Man is 'a working of the soul in the way of excellence' (virtue).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle analogizes to artisans and performers: just as a good harp-player plays well, the good human lives/acts in accord with reason and excellence. This ties happiness to activity (practice) not mere possession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happiness as activity (not mere state)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a difference between possessing a state (habit) and exercising it; the good is in the working/doing, not merely in the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a man may have the habit of virtue but be asleep and not benefit; Olympic winners are selected among those who enter (act), not merely the strongest in potential. Thus happiness requires enacted virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness / duration (a complete life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness requires a complete life; a single day or short period does not make a man blessed and happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because fortunes change, happiness must be judged over a whole life-span; many changes can mar blessedness, so completeness and sufficient length are necessary for proper judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Virtue/Excellence (moral and intellectual) as central elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Some hold happiness to be virtue (excellence), practical wisdom, or scientific philosophy; working in the way of excellence belongs to excellence and so to happiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle's account agrees that virtue is essential: the activities corresponding to excellence are constitutive of happiness. Both moral and intellectual virtues are considered; there is discussion of different views and combinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleasure integrated but not identical with happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure is not identical with Happiness, but the life of virtuous action is in itself pleasant to the virtuous person; noble actions involve pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The multitude equate happiness with pleasure, but Aristotle argues that virtuous actions are inherently pleasant to the person of virtue, so pleasure accompanies happiness rather than constituting it alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: External goods as instruments (necessary but not primary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain external goods (friends, money, political influence, good birth, offspring, physical beauty) are required as instruments and their deficiency can mar blessedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle recognizes that without some external goods it is difficult or impossible to perform noble actions; however, these are secondary instruments, not constitutive of happiness itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between independent (final) goods and instrumental goods
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate independent goods (pursued for their own sakes) from instrumental goods (valued because they produce or preserve other goods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle asks which goods are truly independent (e.g., wisdom, seeing, certain pleasures, honours) and which are pursued for further ends; this taxonomy underpins his account of the Chief Good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability/abiding character of happiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness should be relatively stable and abiding through life; the virtuous person's activities and intellectual pursuits make happiness more continuous than transient fortunes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because working in the way of virtue and the sciences is abiding, the happy person remains steadfast through ordinary misfortunes and bears great mischance nobly. Only great and numerous evils can mar blessedness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of complete virtue (not partial) and sufficiency for acting one's part
rubrics_metrics.description: To be happy one must possess complete virtue and be furnished with sufficient external goods for acting his part in the drama of life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Partial virtue or lack of necessary external conditions prevents full blessedness; Aristotle stresses both completeness of character and adequate circumstances over a life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that death align with life (appropriate end)
rubrics_metrics.description: Happiness is an end and complete; for full account one must consider whether a person's death is in keeping with such a life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because future events can affect assessments, Aristotle raises whether a happy life must also end appropriately — the prospect of a dishonourable death can complicate whether one is judged happy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Question of learnability / habituation versus divine gift or chance
rubrics_metrics.description: Inquiry whether Happiness is learned/acquired by habituation/discipline, or is a gift of the gods or pure chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle leans to the view that through virtue and learning (discipline) happiness can be widely participated in, though he acknowledges the debate and the role of fortune and the gods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodological guidance: begin with what is known; difference between reasoning from and to principles
rubrics_metrics.description: One must start inquiry from what is known (either what we do know or what we may know), and distinguish reasoning from first principles vs. to first principles; training in habits is necessary to study ethical principles profitably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aristotle emphasizes practical starting points, the role of habituation and induction/perception in acquiring first principles, and not demanding the same exactness in all subjects — fit precision to subject-matter.
